question: On a route from Calcutta to Singapore in January, the low-level wind is mainly:

options.text: North-easterly, from the north-east monsoon
South-westerly, from the south-west monsoon
Westerly, from the subtropical jet
Variable, under the ITCZ

explanation: Outflow from the Siberian high sets up the north-east monsoon over the whole route, with the ITCZ lying further south.

question: In January, weather on the northern part of the Calcutta–Singapore route is generally:

options.text: Disrupted by cyclones crossing the coast every day
Foggy for most of the day over the delta
Very poor, with continuous thunderstorms over the sea
Good, as the monsoon air has had a long, dry land track

explanation: Calcutta and Bangladesh are sheltered by the Himalayas, and the air arriving over Burma is dry. Further south, the monsoon picks up moisture over the Gulf of Thailand and South China Sea.

question: In January, the north-east monsoon brings heavy orographic cumulus and thunderstorms to:

options.text: The foothills of the Himalayas
Calcutta and the Ganges delta
The east coasts and central highlands of West Malaysia
The west coast of Burma facing the Bay of Bengal, and the Arakan mountains

explanation: Arriving warm and moist off the South China Sea, the monsoon is lifted over the Malaysian mountains. West coasts are more sheltered.

question: In July, flying conditions on the Calcutta–Singapore route are generally:

options.text: Affected mainly by dust carried from Africa by the Harmattan
Poor, as the moist south-west monsoon gives storms on windward coasts
Excellent, with clear skies and no convection anywhere along the route
Affected by freezing rain at low level in the mornings

explanation: The south-west monsoon has a long sea track; where it reaches the coasts of Bangladesh, Burma, Thailand and Malaysia, orographic lifting triggers severe weather.

question: The ITCZ crosses Singapore northbound in about:

options.text: Never, because it stays north of Singapore
January, returning southbound in July
July, returning southbound across Singapore in January
March, returning southbound in November–December

explanation: Over this route the ITCZ moves north in spring (Singapore March, Calcutta May) and south in autumn (Calcutta October, Singapore November/December).

question: Tropical revolving storms in the Bay of Bengal are called:

options.text: Cyclones, mainly in early and late summer when the ITCZ is over the sea
Willy-willies, mainly in December over the southern bay
Hurricanes, mainly in July when the monsoon is strongest
Typhoons, mainly in midwinter when the north-east monsoon blows over the bay

explanation: In July the ITCZ lies over the land, so the main cyclone periods are around May–June and October–November.

question: In July, the tropical easterly jet over Rangoon is centred near:

options.text: The surface, as a monsoon squall
150 hPa, with speeds around 70 kt
300 hPa, with speeds around 150 kt
850 hPa, with speeds around 20 kt

explanation: Summer heating of Asia reverses the north–south temperature gradient aloft, producing strong upper easterlies at about FL450.

question: On the Calcutta–Singapore route, the tropopause averages about 56 000 ft and the freezing level about:

options.text: 4000 ft in winter
30 000 ft in summer
16 000 ft all year
The surface in January

explanation: The deep, warm tropical troposphere keeps both high all year.

question: The Crachin affecting Hong Kong and the South China coast between January and April is:

options.text: A dust storm carried south from the Gobi desert
Fog, low stratus and drizzle as warm moist air crosses cooler coastal water
A strong, cold northerly wind with clear skies and very good visibility along the coast
The main season of typhoons approaching from the Philippines

explanation: When the wind veers and its source moves over the warm Kuroshio current, the moist air is cooled over the colder coastal sea, giving very poor visibility.

question: From October to December, weather at Hong Kong is usually:

options.text: Foggy and drizzly every day
Snowy
Fine and dry, with excellent visibility
Affected by daily thunderstorms from the ITCZ

explanation: After the ITCZ passes south in September, Hong Kong is sheltered from the dry north-east monsoon by the land to the north.

question: In winter, very cold air from Siberia crossing the Sea of Japan produces:

options.text: Snow showers on Japan's north-west coast and mountains, drier at Tokyo
Fog and drizzle at Tokyo, with clear skies on the north-west coast
Clear skies over the whole of Japan, with severe frost
Typhoons crossing Japan from the Sea of Japan

explanation: The cold air is warmed and moistened over the sea, and orographic lift adds to the instability. The lee side, including Tokyo, is drier and milder.

question: In winter, the subtropical jet near Japan can reach:

options.text: Only about 30 kt, as it is far from the pole
About 60 kt at most, the minimum for a jet
About 500 kt regularly, every winter
Up to about 300 kt in exceptional cases

explanation: The strong temperature contrast between Siberia and the Pacific produces the strongest jet streams in the world near Japan.

question: The Plum Rains are:

options.text: Spring dust storms carried from Mongolia
Freezing rain over Korea in midwinter
Early summer rains over China as the ITCZ moves north
Winter snowfall over Japan from very cold Siberian air

explanation: The ITCZ reaches southern China around May, bringing a prolonged rainy period.

question: Typhoons affecting southern Japan are most frequent:

options.text: Between July and September
Never
In April only
Between December and February

explanation: Up to about a dozen a year can affect southern Japan, mainly in late summer. The wider season in the western Pacific runs from about May to November.

question: Typhoons generally form in the western Pacific at about 10–15°N and then:

options.text: Move south across the Equator into the Southern Hemisphere
Drift west at 10–15 kt around the subtropical high, often recurving north
Move directly eastwards across the Pacific towards Central America and Mexico
Remain stationary near the Equator until they decay

explanation: They are steered by the easterly flow on the southern side of the North Pacific subtropical high and may curve north and north-east as they reach its western edge.

question: Extensive sea fog east of northern Japan in summer is caused by:

options.text: Cold continental air crossing the warm Kuroshio current
Radiation cooling over the land at night
Smoke drifting out to sea from Tokyo
Warm moist air crossing the cold Oyashio current

explanation: As with the Grand Banks, warm air crossing a cold current produces persistent advection fog.

question: On the Singapore–Tokyo route in summer, the upper winds south of about 25°N are mainly:

options.text: Strong northerlies from Siberia
Westerly jet streams of about 150 kt
Light equatorial easterlies of 10–30 kt
Calm at all levels

explanation: In summer the subtropical and polar front jets are little in evidence over the North Pacific.

question: In July, on the route from Singapore to Darwin, the surface wind after crossing the Equator is mainly:

options.text: Strong westerlies of the Roaring Forties
South-easterly trade winds
Calm under the ITCZ
North-westerly monsoon

explanation: In the southern winter the ITCZ is far north. The south-west monsoon at Singapore backs to south-easterly south of the Equator.

question: In the southern winter, visibility south of about 5°S towards Darwin is often reduced by:

options.text: Smoke from forest fires in Siberia
Heavy snow over the Indonesian mountains
Advection fog forming over the Timor Sea and the north coast at night
Haze from dust carried by the south-east trades from Australia

explanation: The trade winds blowing off the dry Australian interior carry dust and haze over the Timor Sea and northern Australia.

question: In January, the ITCZ reaches its most southerly position:

options.text: Just south of Darwin
Over Sydney, on the south-east coast
Over Singapore
Over New Zealand

explanation: It affects the Singapore–Darwin section from about November to March, bringing widespread thunderstorms.

question: In the southern summer, the wind from the South China Sea that crosses the Equator towards northern Australia becomes:

options.text: The north-east monsoon
The south-east trade
The north-west monsoon
The Southerly Buster

explanation: The north-east monsoon backs as it crosses the Equator southbound, becoming north-westerly as far as the ITCZ.

question: Tropical cyclones in the Australian region in summer form over:

options.text: The Coral and Timor Seas near the ITCZ, moving west or curving towards the east coast
The Tasman Sea in winter, moving north towards the Coral Sea and Papua New Guinea
Central Australia in summer, moving outwards towards the coasts in all directions
The Southern Ocean near 50°S, moving north-east across the Tasman Sea

explanation: They form near the ITCZ in January–March and may move west near the north coast, or curve south-east around the South Pacific high to affect Brisbane and sometimes New Zealand.

question: A "Southerly Buster" at Sydney is:

options.text: A hot, dusty north-westerly wind from the interior blowing ahead of a summer cold front
A squally southerly change with a sharp temperature drop behind a summer cold front
A tropical cyclone that reaches Sydney from the Coral Sea
A strong easterly sea breeze that sets in on summer afternoons

explanation: The cold front brings cumulonimbus, squalls and a sharp backing of the wind to the south.

question: Over the Singapore and Indonesia region, convective cloud and thunderstorms are:

options.text: Absent during the southern summer, when the ITCZ is far south
Found only in July, during the south-west monsoon
Rare, because the area lies under the subtropical high
Present most days all year, and enhanced when the ITCZ is overhead

explanation: High temperatures, strong insolation, high humidity and orographic lift make this one of the most thunderstorm-prone areas in the world.

question: In the southern winter, the westerly subtropical jet over Australia lies at about:

options.text: 10°S over Darwin, near 500 hPa, reaching about 50 kt at most
25°S across the continent, near 200 hPa, reaching about 100 kt
The Equator, near 100 hPa, as an easterly jet
50°S over the Southern Ocean, near 850 hPa, at 30 kt

explanation: In summer it moves south to lie along the south coast at a lower speed.

question: Over New Zealand, sea fog can occur off the east coast of the South Island over:

options.text: The Kuroshio current
The warm East Australian current
The cold Antarctic drift current
The Gulf Stream

explanation: Moist air moving over the cold current is cooled to its dew point.

question: On the Cairo–Johannesburg route in January, the northern section from Cairo to about 6°N is:

options.text: Snowy
Very wet, with monsoon rain
Foggy with drizzle
Dry and dusty

explanation: High pressure over the comparatively cool Sahara gives dry, dusty conditions.

question: In January, the ITCZ over eastern Africa lies at its southern extreme over:

options.text: Zimbabwe
Egypt
Kenya's north coast
Sudan

explanation: This brings the wet season to southern Africa, with convection and thunderstorms.

question: In July, Khartoum normally experiences:

options.text: Persistent advection fog from the Red Sea
Its main wet month, as the ITCZ reaches just north of the city
Snow, from cold air drawn south behind the ITCZ
Its driest month of all, as the Sahara high moves south over the city

explanation: The ITCZ brings rain, line squalls and haboobs to central Sudan around July.

question: The Guti is:

options.text: A dusty northerly wind blowing over Egypt and the Sudan ahead of Mediterranean depressions
A warm Föhn wind descending from the highlands of Kenya towards the coast
A south-easterly around the winter high over south-east Africa, bringing stratus to the high veld
A tropical cyclone forming in the Mozambique Channel in the southern summer

explanation: Orographic lifting of the moist south-east trades onto the plateau forms stratus and stratocumulus.

question: At Nairobi, the "Long Rains" occur:

options.text: January, when the Sahara high extends south over Kenya
November to December, after the ITCZ moves south, with dry north-east trades
July, when the ITCZ lies far to the north over Sudan
March to May, after the ITCZ moves north, with moist south-east trades

explanation: The southbound ITCZ in November–December gives the lighter "Short Rains", followed by drier north-east trades from Arabia.

question: Low stratus and fog at Nairobi are most likely:

options.text: Early morning, from easterly winds lifted onto the high plateau
Only in July, when the ITCZ is overhead
Never, because the city is so high
Mid-afternoon, from strong convection over the city and the plateau

explanation: Nairobi lies above 5000 ft, about 200 nm from the coast. Moist easterlies rising to it can produce stratus at the surface between about 0200 and 0800 local time.

question: At Johannesburg in January (southern summer), weather typically includes:

options.text: Clear skies with hard frost every night
Snow on the high veld
Continuous drizzle from low stratus throughout the whole day
Early low cloud or fog, giving way to afternoon cumulus and showers

explanation: It is the wet season. Moist easterly air from the Indian Ocean rising onto the plateau can form early fog, and daytime heating produces showers.

question: On equatorial routes such as Calcutta–Singapore and over Nairobi, the tropopause averages about:

options.text: 56 000 ft all year
26 000 ft in winter
36 000 ft all year
70 000 ft in summer

explanation: The deep tropical troposphere puts the tropopause near 56 000 ft with little seasonal change.

question: On the Calcutta–Singapore route in January, above about 20 000 ft the winds are:

options.text: Strong easterly jet streams blowing along the whole of the route
Westerly near Calcutta, dying away to light easterlies south of 10°N
Calm along the whole route at all levels
North-east monsoon winds at every level

explanation: The upper westerlies overrun the shallow monsoon in the north, giving way to equatorial easterlies further south.

question: Over Singapore, convective cloud and thunderstorms are:

options.text: Rare because the area is under the subtropical high
Absent from June to September
Common in all seasons
Found only in January

explanation: The equatorial climate gives daily convection throughout the year.

question: Industrial haze near large cities on the Singapore–Auckland route, such as Sydney, may reduce visibility to:

options.text: Less than 50 m
More than 50 km
Zero during the day
About 1–2 km

explanation: Smoke haze is trapped under stable conditions near big cities.

question: In the southern summer, the westerly subtropical jet over Australia lies:

options.text: Over central Asia, far from Australia
Along the south coast, at around 70 kt
Over Darwin, at around 150 kt
Over the Equator, as an easterly jet

explanation: In summer the whole continent is hot, so the strongest temperature contrast lies along the south coast.

question: On the Cairo–Nairobi section in July, the surface wind north of the ITCZ near 18°N is mainly:

options.text: South-easterly, the Guti
South-westerly, the summer monsoon flow
Northerly, an extension of the Etesian
Westerly, from the Atlantic

explanation: High pressure over the Mediterranean and low pressure over Arabia drive the northerly flow.

question: Haboobs in northern Sudan are most likely:

options.text: From May to September, by day, as the ITCZ moves
Never, as Sudan has no thunderstorms
Only in December, with the north-east trades
In January, at night, under the Sahara high

explanation: Convective outflows near the ITCZ raise walls of dust, sometimes to 10 000 ft.
